clinicalPearls: Priapism is a prolonged penile erection (typically beyond four hours) unrelated to sexual stimulation, and the critical first step is to distinguish ischaemic (low-flow) from non-ischaemic (high-flow) types

Ischaemic priapism is a painful, rigid erection representing a compartment syndrome of the corpora cavernosa and is a urological emergency because prolonged ischaemia causes fibrosis and permanent erectile dysfunction

Non-ischaemic (high-flow) priapism is usually painless, semi-rigid, and follows perineal or penile trauma with an arteriolar-sinusoidal fistula; it is not an emergency and often resolves or is managed by embolisation
Cavernosal blood gas analysis distinguishes the two: ischaemic blood is dark and hypoxic/acidotic, whereas high-flow blood is bright red with near-arterial values
Common causes of ischaemic priapism include sickle cell disease, haematological malignancy, and drugs, notably intracavernosal vasoactive agents and certain psychotropic and recreational drugs
Emergency management of ischaemic priapism proceeds stepwise from corporal aspiration and irrigation to intracavernosal sympathomimetic injection, and to surgical shunting if these fail
Underlying conditions such as sickle cell disease require concurrent systemic treatment alongside local measures
Stuttering (recurrent) priapism, common in sickle cell disease, warrants preventive strategies to reduce recurrent ischaemic episodes
reference.pathophysiology: Priapism reflects a disturbance of the normal mechanisms that terminate erection. In ischaemic (low-flow) priapism, veno-occlusion persists so blood becomes trapped in the corpora cavernosa, producing stagnant, hypoxic, acidotic blood and a compartment-syndrome-like state; prolonged ischaemia leads to smooth muscle necrosis and corporal fibrosis. Causes include sickle cell disease and other haemoglobinopathies, leukaemic infiltration, and pharmacological agents. Non-ischaemic (high-flow) priapism results from unregulated arterial inflow, typically through a cavernosal artery fistula created by perineal or penile trauma, so oxygenation is maintained and tissue ischaemia does not occur.
additionalDifferentials: Drug-induced erection (intracavernosal agents, psychotropics, recreational drugs)
Sickle cell disease or other haemoglobinopathy
additionalInvestigations: Cavernosal blood gas analysis to differentiate ischaemic from non-ischaemic priapism
Penile colour Doppler ultrasound to assess cavernosal blood flow and identify a fistula
Full blood count and film with haemoglobinopathy screen (sickle cell testing)
Toxicology and medication review for causative agents
Selective pudendal arteriography if embolisation of a high-flow fistula is planned
redFlags: Ischaemic priapism is a urological emergency; delay leads to corporal fibrosis and permanent erectile dysfunction
A rigid, painful erection persisting beyond four hours
Underlying sickle cell crisis or haematological malignancy requiring urgent systemic treatment
Failure of aspiration and intracavernosal therapy, mandating urgent surgical shunting
reference.prognosis: Prompt relief of ischaemic priapism improves the chance of preserved erectile function, but episodes lasting many hours frequently result in fibrosis and long-term erectile dysfunction; non-ischaemic priapism has a benign course and often resolves spontaneously or after embolisation.
pitfalls: Failing to distinguish ischaemic from non-ischaemic priapism before treatment, leading to inappropriate management
Delaying emergency intervention in ischaemic priapism and risking irreversible fibrosis
Overlooking an underlying cause such as sickle cell disease or a causative medication
Treating high-flow priapism as an emergency with aggressive corporal procedures
Neglecting preventive management of recurrent stuttering priapism
management: Urgently distinguish ischaemic from non-ischaemic priapism using cavernosal blood gas analysis and colour Doppler to direct therapy
For ischaemic priapism, perform corporal aspiration and saline irrigation followed by intracavernosal sympathomimetic injection such as phenylephrine
Proceed to surgical shunting, and consider early penile prosthesis in prolonged refractory cases, when aspiration and sympathomimetics fail
Treat the underlying cause, including hydration, oxygenation and exchange transfusion for sickle cell disease and withdrawal of causative drugs
Manage non-ischaemic priapism conservatively or with selective arterial embolisation of the cavernosal fistula
Provide analgesia and address the corporal compartment-syndrome state
Refer emergently to urology, with haematology input for haemoglobinopathy-related disease
Counsel on recurrence and erectile dysfunction, and consider prophylaxis for recurrent or stuttering priapism
